title: Your rule of life
hookLine: write the rule you'll keep after the summit
tomorrow: what happens when someone blesses you out loud, by name?

lines: STRICTER, OR NO PLAN AT ALL?
cards: Habit apps love a streak, and then one missed Tuesday breaks it. Some people answer with a stricter plan. Some give up on plans altogether.
Christians have weighed the same choice for a long time, around something called a rule of life: a few written lines for how you'll pray and live. And both sides can quote the same letter of Paul's.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: A PATH TO WALK BY.
teach.b: View one: a rule is a path under your feet. Near the end of Galatians, Paul writes, "And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy." Walk according to.
Benedict wrote a rule for monks, and in its last chapter calls it a little rule for beginners.
On this view, a few plain lines kept on hard days carry you when feelings don't. View two: careful, a rule can become a cage.
Earlier in that same letter, Paul writes, "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage."
On this view grace comes first, and a rule kept to earn God's favor has missed the point. Each side has a fair case. The first can say that freedom without a path tends to drift.
The second can say that a path without freedom turns into a ledger.

And both keep Paul's picture of himself from another letter: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." He never claims to have arrived.
So a rule written near a summit isn't a trophy for five years done. It's a few plain lines for tomorrow morning, and the one after that.

how: Monastic communities live by a written rule, such as Benedict's, and some Christians outside monasteries write a short personal rule of daily and weekly practice, sometimes with a friend or spiritual director.

games.q: what does “your rule of life” mean?
o: a few written lines for how you'll pray and live
a vow to give away everything you own
the official law code of a national church

games.q: your rule of life — tap the pairs.

s: a rule of life is only for monks and nuns
Benedict wrote for monks, but some Christians outside monasteries keep short personal rules.
both views in today's debate can quote Paul's letter to the Galatians
'walk according to this rule' (6:16) and 'stand fast… in the liberty' (5:1).
in Philippians, Paul says he has already arrived
he presses toward the mark, forgetting what's behind, reaching for what's ahead.

games.q: a friend says, "if you don't keep a strict daily rule, you're not serious about your faith." give the best case for the other view.
o: rules are only for beginners, so serious believers outgrow them.
Paul: stand fast in the liberty; a rule kept to earn favor becomes a yoke.
God doesn't notice what people do day to day anyway.
games.why: the caution comes from Galatians 5:1: 'be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.' the same letter also blesses 'as many as walk according to this rule' (6:16). both views are Paul's.

practice: The prophet Habakkuk was told, "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it."

Take a card and write three short lines: one for each day, one for each week, one for the people in your life, each small enough to keep on a hard day. Then set it where you'll see it, by the mirror, the kettle or the door.

wordCard.voice: Your rule of life. A few plain lines for the day, the week and the people around you, written to keep after the summit.

orig.note: Greek: a rule, a standard to walk by. the word behind 'this rule' in Galatians 6:16.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the rule goes on, because Paul never claims to have arrived. Until tomorrow.
